etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English whirlen, contracted from earlier *whirvelen, *whervelen, possibly from Old English *hwyrflian, *hweorflian (attested in hwirflung, hwerflung (“change, vicissitude”)), frequentative form of Old English hweorfan (“to turn”), itself from Proto-West Germanic *hwerban, from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną (“to turn”); or perhaps from Old Norse hvirfla (“to go round, spin”). Cognate with Dutch wervelen (“to whirl, swirl”), German wirbeln (“to whirl, swirl”), Danish hvirvle (“to whirl”), Swedish virvla (older spelling hvirfla), Albanian vorbull (“a whirl”). Related to whirr and wharve.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To rotate, revolve, spin or turn rapidly.

quote.citation: 1900 May 17, L[yman] Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chicago, Ill.; New York, N.Y.: Geo[rge] M[elvin] Hill Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: The house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air. Dorothy felt as if she were going up in a balloon.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To have a sensation of spinning or reeling.

quote.citation: 1861, E. J. Guerin, Mountain Charley, page 13:
quote.text: My brained [sic] whirled as he went on, but yet there was a fearful impression that the worst was not told.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make something or someone whirl.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He whirls his sword around without delay.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To remove or carry quickly with, or as with, a revolving motion; to snatch.

quote.citation: c. 1630, John Milton, “The Passion”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC:
quote.text: See, see the chariot, and those rushing wheels, / That whirled the prophet up at Chebar flood.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XV, page 24:
quote.text: To-night the winds begin to rise⁠And roar from yonder dropping day:⁠The last red leaf is whirl’d away,The rooks are blown about the skies; […]

quote.citation: 1855, Alfred Tennyson, “(please specify the page)”, in Maud, and Other Poems, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The passionate heart of the poet is whirl’d into folly.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English whirl, wherwille, whorwhil, wervel, from Old English hwirfel, hwyrfel (“whirlpool”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwirbil, from Proto-Germanic *hwirbilaz, *hwarbilaz (“swirl, whirl, whirlpool”), equivalent to wharve +‎ -el; and also Old Norse hvirfill (“ring, circle, crown”), whence Danish hvirvel (“cowlick”), Dutch werveling (“whirling, vortex”), German Low German Warvel (“whirl, whirlpool”), German Wirbel (“whirl, whirlpool”).

definitions.definition: (informal) (usually following “give”) A brief experiment or trial.
